newsitem.title: UK: Glaxo to stress respiratory growth prospect.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo to stress respiratory growth prospect.

text.p: Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc (GW) told Reuters on Friday it was preparing to present a series of academic papers which it believes reinforce prospects for further rapid growth in its 1.8 billion stg respiratory drug portfolio.

Presentations to the six-day American Thoracic Society conference which starts later on Friday in San Francisco will underline measurable improvements in quality of life for asthma sufferers who use the group's long-acting quick-relief drug Serevent.

But the company said it also believes Serevent can help to prevent the onset of asthma attacks and has significant potential in treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a rapid deterioration in lung function which affects around 20 percent of all smokers.
Glaxo Wellcome already dominates the world market for respiratory drugs, accounting for more than a quarter of world-wide sales.

But the sector has taken on a new significance in recent weeks, with respiratory sales overtaking GW's gastro-intestinal products for the first time as anti-ulcer blockbuster Zantac goes into off-patent decline.
Respiratory diseases director Darrell Baker told Reuters the portfolio was capable of "long-term sustainable growth and will be one of the cornerstones of the business through the next decade".

GW's dominance of the asthma market was built up steadily over nearly three decades on the back of the old warhorse Ventolin, launched in 1969 but still its best-selling respiratory product with sales of 471 million stg last year.

Since its introduction in 1990, the bronchodilator Serevent has seen rapid growth, with sales jumping 29 percent to 349 million stg in 1996. Baker said the drug was targeted at "regular relief of symptoms, but it is a molecule which we are still discovering a great deal about".
The inhaled corticosteroid Flixotide/Flovent, which is used to combat the inflammation at the root of asthma, saw sales double last year to 185 million stg.

Serevent has already won a quality of life indication in the U.S, the first drug ever to do so, because of measurable improvements in areas like easing persistent symptoms and helping sufferers to sleep through the night.
However GW's director of respiratory medicine Rick Fuller said evidence to be presented in San Francisco would indicate that "Serevent is having a positive effect" on the onset of attacks.
Scientists working in New Zealand found that patients given Serevent had almost half the incidence of asthma attacks of those given GW's Ventolin (salbutamol) or a placebo.
A second paper at the conference will show that Serevent also significantly reduced the need for inhaled corticosteroids, which have varying degrees of side effects.

At its research update on May 2, GW announced plans for a new drug combining Serevent and Flixotide/Flovent, which it believes will combine the benefits of both while reducing the amount of each drug needed.
The other main plank of GW's strategy will be COPD, where around one-third of Serevent sales are targeted. Fuller believes the proportion will "rise substantially".

COPD is estimated to affect one-fifth of all smokers, and is always fatal. The numbers afflicted in developing countries in particular are expected to rocket in the next decade, and GW points to figures showing that virtually the entire male Chinese population smokes.

The market for COPD drugs is already nearly as large as that for asthma, totalling 2.37 billion stg a year against 2.59 billion stg for asthma. But most of this is taken up by antibiotics and cough and cold-type remedies.

GW told Reuters that data to be presented in San Francisco would show Serevent significantly improved lung function in COPD patients compared with placebo and the drug ipratropium, versions of which are sold by Sweden's Astra AB and Germany's Boehringer Ingelheim.
Other recent research has indicated that Flixotide may be the first inhaled steroid to demonstrate improved lung function in COPD, with the improvement sustained over a six month period.
"It is clearly a very important disease which in the minds of healthcare workers was essentially untreatable," said Fuller. "We are moving from can-do-nothing to can-do-something."
Fuller added: "Serevent, as in asthma, can produce long-term improvements in lung function in COPD. That means people will be able to get about more and lead a better life."
Later this year GW will publish results of trials to test whether Serevent can attack the underlying disease as well as the symptoms.
